title: Disparity in the classroom and what I’m going to do about it o-about-it/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, a science teacher and tutor, reflects on how unevenly her students used the lockdown period and what she plans to do on their return. Tutor interviews showed that even well-behaved, well-supported students had no routine, slept and ate poorly and mostly did not read. She concludes, while admitting the evidence is anecdotal, that structure and routine explained who coped. Her worry is a new gap between students who kept a routine and those who did not. She then sets out concrete plans at two levels: as a tutor she will run reading and discussion time and follow up on every behaviour point and achievement, and as a teacher she will enforce lesson-start routines, rigorous homework follow-up, adapted booklets, and equitable access to resources. It is a practical, honest return-to-school plan with a clear thesis.
points: Hidden disparity can sit among compliant, well-behaved students, so the quiet ones are worth checking on.
Castelino attributes poor coping to missing daily structure, while acknowledging this is anecdotal.
As a tutor, she plans to build a routine of shared reading and discussion of current learning and news.
As a teacher, she plans strict lesson-start routines, relentless follow-up of missed homework and a higher bar for quality of submitted work.
She plans to address digital inequality discreetly by finding who lacked devices or internet and giving them hard copies.
quotes: I want to talk about how little some students did during lockdown. I am well aware this may be linked to the disparity I see in other aspects of their lives. However, this is not always the case.
I was shocked to find that most were not really coping well at all. They didn’t say as much.

The main difference that I think resulted in these poor choices was a lack of structure and routine. To give credence to this conclusion, I found that the students that had a set structure to their day (wake up at around the same time, work for a set amount of time, go out for a walk/run, sleep at a reasonable time) were happy and were mostly on top of their home learning.
It does make me worry that when we return, we will see a new disparity amongst our students: those that followed a routine and were able to cope with the work, and those that didn’t.
Once again, a good routine will need to be established and strictly followed with each class. This will include a routine for the starts of lessons.

As well as being very strict with the submission of homework, I now plan to be relentless about the quality of submitted work. I will be the first to admit that I have been lax about this in the past.
Everything else I do in the classroom should be as usual. Simply being in school will be different to the structure-less home learning attempted by many students.
